ai.literal: Virtue he speaks not, evil things even if he does, a person 'back he speaks not' saying is sweet.
ai.translation: Even if a person does not speak of virtue and commits evil deeds, it is good to be able to say that he does not backbite.
ai.modern: ஒருவன் அறத்தைப் பற்றிப் பேசாமல் பாவச் செயல்களைச் செய்தாலும், அவன் மற்றவர்களைப் பற்றிப் புறம் பேசமாட்டான் என்று சொல்லப்படுவது அவனுக்கு நல்லதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet emphasizes the severe nature of backbiting by comparing it to other moral failings. It states that even if someone completely ignores virtuous speech and actively commits bad deeds, refraining from speaking ill behind others' backs remains a redeeming quality. The word 'புறம்' refers to the back, meaning speaking behind someone's back. The poet suggests that avoiding this specific flaw brings a distinct sweetness or goodness ('இனிது') to a person's character.

ai.literal: Virtue having destroyed, unvirtuous things than doing, worse indeed: behind the back having slandered, having acted falsely smiling.
ai.translation: Smiling falsely to someone's face while destroying their reputation behind their back is worse than abandoning virtue and committing evil deeds.
ai.modern: அறத்தை அழித்து பாவங்களைச் செய்வதை விட, ஒருவருக்குப் பின்னால் அவரைப் பற்றி அவதூறு பேசிவிட்டு நேரில் பொய்யாகச் சிரிப்பது மிகவும் தீமையானதாகும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet compares two types of wrongdoing to highlight the severity of backbiting. The first line describes a person who abandons virtue and commits evil deeds. The second line states that it is even worse to destroy someone's reputation behind their back and then smile falsely to their face. The repetition of the word 'aḻīi' (having destroyed) powerfully links the destruction of abstract virtue with the destruction of a person's good name, showing that deceitful slander is the greater evil.

ai.literal: Having backbitten, having acted falsely, than living life, dying, virtue's decree even, benefit will give.
ai.translation: Dying is better than living a false life by backbiting; such a death will yield the very benefits promised by the decree of virtue.
ai.modern: புறங்கூறிப் பொய்த்து வாழும் வாழ்க்கையை விட இறந்து விடுவது மேல்; அந்த மரணம் அறநூல்கள் கூறும் நன்மைகளைத் தரும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet strongly condemns the cowardly act of backbiting while pretending to be a friend. It states that dying is far better than leading such a false, deceitful life. Choosing death over a life of backbiting is so noble that it will bestow the very blessings and wealth that the decrees of virtue promise.

ai.literal: Standing before the eyes without kindness even if [one] speaks, let [one] not speak without being in front words that do not look behind.
ai.translation: Even if you speak mercilessly to someone's face, do not speak thoughtless words behind their back.
ai.modern: ஒருவருக்கு நேரே நின்று இரக்கமில்லாமல் கடுமையாகப் பேசினாலும் பேசலாம், ஆனால் அவர் இல்லாதபோது பின்விளைவுகளை எண்ணாமல் அவரைப் பற்றிப் புறங்கூறக் கூடாது.
ai.explanation: This couplet contrasts harsh direct speech with the cowardice of backbiting. The word 'கண்ணின்று' (standing before the eyes) refers to speaking directly to someone's face, even if done 'கண்ணற' (without kindness or consideration). While such harshness is not ideal, the poet states it is far worse to speak 'முன்னின்று' (without being in front, meaning in their absence). One must never speak words behind someone's back that fail to consider the future consequences ('பின்நோக்காச் சொல்').

ai.literal: Virtue speaking he-of-the-heart absence back speaking by-meanness to-see will-be.
ai.translation: A person's lack of a truly virtuous heart is clearly revealed by the meanness of their backbiting.
ai.modern: ஒருவன் அறத்தைப் பற்றிப் பேசினாலும், அவனது நெஞ்சத்தில் உண்மையில் அறம் இல்லை என்பது அவன் மற்றவர்களைப் பற்றிப் புறங்கூறும் சிறுமைக் குணத்தால் வெளிப்படும்.
ai.explanation: This couplet explains how the habit of backbiting exposes a person's true character. Even if someone constantly speaks about virtue, their inner lack of a virtuous heart (அன்மை) is betrayed by their actions. The meanness of slandering others behind their backs serves as visible proof of their inner emptiness.

ai.literal: Another's fault he-who-speaks, his-own fault even-among, the-worst-kind having-selected to-be-spoken will-happen.
ai.translation: If a man speaks of another's faults, his own faults will be sifted through and the worst of them will be exposed.
ai.modern: மற்றொருவனுடைய பழியைப் பற்றிப் பேசுபவனுடைய சொந்தப் பழிகளுக்குள்ளும், மிகவும் கடுமையானவற்றை ஆராய்ந்து தேர்ந்தெடுத்து மற்றவர்கள் பேசுவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: This couplet warns of the inevitable retaliation that comes from backbiting. The word 'கூறுவான்' refers to one who habitually points out the faults of others. In response, others will not merely point out his faults, but will examine them ('தெரிந்து') to find the most severe or damaging ones ('திறன்') among all his flaws ('தன்பழி உள்ளும்'). Thus, speaking ill of others guarantees that one's own worst flaws will be exposed to the world.

ai.literal: To divide having spoken, friends they will separate; to rejoice having spoken, engaging in friendship those who do not know.
ai.translation: Those who do not know how to speak pleasantly and cultivate friendship will speak divisively and alienate even their own friends.
ai.modern: மகிழும்படி பேசி நட்புச் செய்வதை அறியாதவர்கள், நண்பர்களுக்கிடையே பிளவு உண்டாகும்படி புறங்கூறி அவர்களைப் பிரித்துவிடுவார்கள்.
ai.explanation: The couplet contrasts two ways of speaking and their social consequences. The phrase 'நகச் சொல்லி' means speaking in a way that brings joy, which is the foundation of building friendship ('நட்பு ஆடல்'). Those who lack this skill ('தேற்றாதவர்') resort to backbiting. By speaking divisively ('பகச் சொல்லி'), they end up alienating even their own close friends ('கேளிர்'). The verse highlights that backbiting stems from an inability to foster positive relationships.

ai.literal: Close friends' faults even, spreading, those of the habit - what indeed strangers towards?
ai.translation: If people have the habit of broadcasting even the faults of their close friends, what will they do to strangers?
ai.modern: நெருங்கிய நண்பர்களின் குற்றங்களையே ஊரறியத் தூற்றும் பழக்கம் உடையவர்கள், முன்பின் தெரியாத அயலாரிடம் என்னதான் செய்வார்களோ?
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the destructive and untrustworthy nature of those who habitually backbite. The word 'துன்னியார்' refers to close, intimate friends, while 'ஏதிலார்' means strangers or outsiders. The poet asks a rhetorical question: if someone is willing to expose and spread ('தூற்றும்') even the flaws of their closest companions, what limits would they have when dealing with strangers? It warns that a slanderer spares no one.

ai.literal: Virtue having considered, will bear I wonder the earth, back having looked mean words he who speaks' burden.
ai.translation: I wonder if it is only out of a sense of duty to virtue that the earth bears the burden of a man who waits behind someone's back to speak mean words.
ai.modern: ஒருவர் இல்லாத நேரம் பார்த்து அவரைப் பற்றி இழிவான சொற்களைப் பேசுபவனுடைய உடல் பாரத்தை, இதுவும் ஒரு தர்மம் என்று கருதித்தான் இந்தப் பூமி சுமக்கிறதோ?
ai.explanation: This couplet marvels at the earth's patience in supporting the weight of a backbiter. The earth is traditionally praised for bearing all burdens, but the poet wonders if it only tolerates the backbiter out of a strict adherence to its duty (அறன்). The phrase 'புறன் நோக்கி' (looking at the back) vividly captures the cowardice of waiting for someone's absence to speak ill of them. By calling the backbiter a 'பொறை' (burden), the couplet emphasizes that such a person is nothing but dead weight on the world.

ai.literal: Strangers' fault like, one's own fault if able to see, evil is there [question] for enduring life?
ai.translation: If people could see their own faults just as they see the faults of others, would any harm ever come to their enduring lives?
ai.modern: மற்றவர்களுடைய குற்றத்தைப் பார்ப்பது போலத் தன்னுடைய குற்றத்தையும் ஒருவனால் பார்க்க முடியுமானால், நிலைபெற்ற இந்த உயிருக்கு ஏதேனும் துன்பம் வருமா?
ai.explanation: This couplet highlights the common human tendency to easily spot the flaws in others while ignoring one's own. It asks a rhetorical question: if a person develops the ability to examine their own faults as critically as they do a stranger's, could any evil befall them? The word 'காண்கிற்பின்' emphasizes the rare ability and effort required to truly see oneself. By turning the critical eye inward, a person avoids the harm that comes from ignorance and backbiting, ensuring a peaceful existence.
